script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Good evening, welcome to the Lakeside Hotel. Do you have a reservation?

script.speaker: Guest
script.text: Yes, under Ortega. I booked a double room for three nights, from the twenty-first.

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: I see the booking. Unfortunately the double room is not ready. There's a problem with the heating in that wing.

script.speaker: Guest
script.text: That's frustrating. I was told I'd have a room with a lake view.

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: I'm sorry. We can offer a twin room on the third floor. It also has a lake view, but it will be available only from nine tomorrow morning.

script.speaker: Guest
script.text: So where would I stay tonight?

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: We'll pay for a room at the Harbour Inn, two streets away. Breakfast is included there.

script.speaker: Guest
script.text: Fine. Will I be able to get back to the hotel tomorrow?

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Yes, a taxi will collect you from the Harbour Inn at eight-thirty and bring you here.

script.speaker: Guest
script.text: Thanks. Can I have the room charge removed for tonight, then?

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Of course. The room is free for tonight, and you'll also receive a voucher worth fifteen pounds for the restaurant.

script.speaker: Guest
script.text: Is there a gym I can use?

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Yes, the gym is on the lower ground floor. It's open from six in the morning until ten at night.

script.speaker: Guest
script.text: And the pool?

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: The pool is open until eight. Towels are available at the pool entrance.

script.speaker: Guest
script.text: Can I get a late breakfast?

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Breakfast finishes at ten-thirty, but room service is available all day.

script.speaker: Guest
script.text: Good. Is there Wi-Fi in the rooms?

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Yes, the password is printed on your key card holder.

script.speaker: Guest
script.text: One more question: is there an airport shuttle?

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Yes, it runs every hour from the front entrance. Enjoy your stay.

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Would you like help with your luggage to the room?

script.speaker: Guest
script.text: Yes, please. Thank you for your help.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Coming up on the station, here's everything you need to know about this year's Riverside Music Festival.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: The festival runs for three days, from the fourteenth to the sixteenth of July, in Hartley Park. Gates open at noon each day.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: There are four stages this year. The biggest is the Riverside Stage, which holds about eight thousand people.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Tickets are available online or from the box office in the high street. A day ticket costs twenty-five pounds, and a weekend pass costs sixty.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Under-sixteens go free when accompanied by an adult, but they must have a ticket with a valid ID.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Parking is limited, so we recommend the park-and-ride service from the leisure centre. It runs every fifteen minutes.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Please note that glass bottles are not allowed inside the park. Water refill points are available near every stage.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Finally, the festival is cancelled in the event of severe weather, and refunds will be issued in full.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Before we go, a quick reminder about the children's area. The Little Acre zone offers face painting, puppet shows and craft tents, and it is staffed by trained volunteers all day.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Food traders will be serving dishes from around the world, with a special vegetarian village near the east gate. Prices are displayed clearly, and card payments are accepted at most stalls.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Accessibility matters to us. There are step-free routes between all stages, accessible toilets near the main gate, and a quiet area for visitors who need a break from the crowds.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: If you're travelling by train, the nearest station is a ten-minute walk from the park. Taxis queue outside the station, but drivers can drop off only at the south entrance.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Volunteers are needed for the litter patrols. Sign up at the information tent, which opens at nine each morning.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Thanks for listening. Stay tuned for the full line-up announcement later this week, and we'll see you in the park.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Ben, have you looked at the site plan for the library project? I'm worried about the entrance.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: Yes. The current design puts the entrance on the busy road side, which is noisy.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Exactly. I think we should move it to the quieter courtyard, even though that adds a corridor.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: The corridor would cost extra, but the acoustics would improve a lot. Did you run the sound model?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Yes, the model shows a reduction of about ten decibels in the reading rooms if we do that.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: That's a big difference. What about daylight? The reading room faces north.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: North is actually good for steady light, without glare. But the east windows need shading.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: Agreed. We could add external louvres. They're cheaper than tinted glass.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Let's check the budget first. The client has capped the materials spend at four hundred thousand pounds.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: Then we might have to drop the rooftop garden if the louvres push us over.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Maybe. I'll draft the revised plan, and we'll show it to the client on Friday the sixth.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: Did the structural engineer confirm the louvre fixings will work?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Yes, she sent a note yesterday. The fixings are fine on the north elevation, but the east side needs reinforced brackets.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: That adds cost again. Can we use the same bracket design as the lecture hall?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Probably not, because the wall thickness is different. I'll ask her to check.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: Okay. What about the planting scheme for the courtyard?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: The landscape team proposed native grasses, which are low maintenance and suit the local climate.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: Good. That keeps running costs down, which the client will like.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Exactly. Let's keep the plan simple and clear for the presentation.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: Agreed. I'll update the drawings tonight.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Thanks, Ben.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: This week's lecture covers coral reef monitoring, a field that depends on long-term data to detect change.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they support roughly a quarter of all known marine species.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Many people living on the coast also depend on reefs, since they provide food and act as natural barriers that reduce the force of waves during storms.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Monitoring teams usually record coral cover, the percentage of the seabed covered by living coral, along fixed transect lines.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Divers also count fish, but the counts are often unreliable because fish move. Video cameras placed on the reef now provide more consistent records.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Recording can continue for long periods, and the footage can be reviewed later by several people, which reduces the chance of individual error.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The biggest threat is bleaching. When water temperatures rise, corals expel the algae that live in their tissues, and they turn white.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Bleached corals can recover if temperatures return to normal quickly, but prolonged heat often kills them.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Local pressures such as sewage and overfishing make the situation worse, because they weaken reefs before the heat arrives.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: For your assignment, use the reef dataset from the university portal, and remember to report the sampling depth for each transect.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Note that the dataset comes from several different teams, so you should read the notes that accompany each file before you start your analysis.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Let's consider how reefs recover after a bleaching event. Recovery depends on several factors, including the number of healthy corals nearby that can supply new larvae to the damaged area.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Fish populations also play a role. Herbivorous fish graze on algae, which keeps seaweed from covering the reef surface and gives new coral larvae space to settle.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Scientists have tested the use of heat-tolerant coral strains in restoration projects. Early results are encouraging, but the long-term survival of these corals is still uncertain.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Another approach is to move healthy fragments from one site to another, but this is slow and expensive, so it is only practical for small areas.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Local communities are important partners in monitoring. Fishing cooperatives often notice changes in reef health before scientists do, and their observations can guide survey priorities.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Data quality matters enormously. Every survey should record the date, the tide level, the depth and the observer's name, so that results from different years can be compared fairly.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Training is part of this too: volunteers need clear instructions so that everyone records things in the same way.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Remember that monitoring is not an end in itself. The purpose is to inform management decisions, such as where to set up marine protected areas and how to regulate fishing.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Next week we'll look at satellite monitoring, which can cover entire regions but cannot yet detect fine detail on individual corals. Please complete the reading on remote sensing in the course reader, and bring a short summary of one method to share with the group. The assignment rubric is posted on the course page, and it gives the weighting for each section.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Late submissions will not be accepted without a medical note. Your tutor will confirm the deadline by email.
